title: The Offering That Goes Up in Smoke
sum: From inside the tent that his glory has just filled, God calls Moses and begins to teach how ordinary Israelites may come near. The first offering is the burnt offering: a flawless male from the cattle, the sheep or goats, or, for those with little, a pair of birds. The worshiper leans his hand on the animal, slaughters, skins and cuts it up; the priests splash the blood around the altar and make the whole animal go up in smoke, "a soothing smell for the LORD."

The chapter is spare and repetitive, but it sets the pattern for the whole book: the person presents an offering, God accepts it, and atonement is made. The same words close the bull, the sheep and the bird. What matters is not the size of the offering but that it is wholly given.
readings: Read as worship

The burnt offering is a gift in which the giver keeps nothing back. Jewish and Christian devotional readers see in it the giving of the whole self, which Paul calls "a living sacrifice" (Romans 12:1).
Read as atonement

Because 1:4 says the offering is "accepted for him, to make atonement for him," many readers, from Ramban to modern evangelical commentators, see substitution: the animal's life given in place of the worshiper's.
Read as a meal for God

Anthropologists and historians of religion note the shared Near Eastern idea of feeding the gods (see 3:11) and read the language of "food" and "smell" as old terms that Israel kept and reinterpreted.

views.H: A real ritual given at Sinai for Israel's worship in the wilderness and later at the temple. The opening ties Leviticus to Exodus 40: the voice now comes from the tent.
views.C: The opening of the Priestly manual of sacrifice (chapters 1–7), probably drawn from temple practice and edited by priestly writers. The lay-centered order of chapters 1–5 may have been written for worshipers, the priest-centered 6–7 for clergy.
views.A: The leaning of the hand, the division of the body, the burning of the whole: a ritual of giving and transformation, in which smoke carries the offering from the human world to God's.
views.J: The book children traditionally began with. After AD 70 the rabbis taught that prayer and study replace the offerings (Hosea 14:2; Menachot 110a), and the morning prayers still recite the sacrificial laws.
views.X: Christians see the burnt offering fulfilled in Christ, who "gave himself up for us, an offering and sacrifice to God, a fragrant smell" (Ephesians 5:2), and in believers offering their bodies as living sacrifices (Romans 12:1).

deep.b:
Scholars have proposed several big theories. E. B. Tylor (1871) saw sacrifice as a gift to win a god's favor. William Robertson Smith (1889) saw it as a communion meal uniting worshipers with their god. Henri Hubert and Marcel Mauss (1898) saw a way to link the sacred and the ordinary through a victim. René Girard (1972) argued that sacrifice channels a community's violence onto a substitute. Each catches something in Leviticus: the burnt offering is a gift, the peace offering a shared meal, the sin offering a cleansing.

Within Judaism, Maimonides and Ramban gave the classic contrasting answers (see the note on 1:2). Within Christianity, the dominant reading has been substitution, the animal standing in for the sinner, fulfilled in Christ (Isaiah 53; Hebrews 9–10), though Eastern Christian and some modern Western theologians stress communion and cleansing more than penalty. Many recent scholars (Milgrom, Gane, Sklar) say no single theory covers all five offerings, and Leviticus itself never explains them in a sentence.

echoes: Exodus 40:34–35; Genesis 8:20–21; Genesis 22:2; Genesis 22:13; Psalm 51:16–19; Psalm 50:8–15; Micah 6:6–8; Romans 12:1; Ephesians 5:2; Hebrews 10:5–10

settings.what: The law of the burnt offering
settings.by: The LORD, calling to Moses from the tent of meeting
settings.to: The Israelites, through Moses (1:2): any Israelite who brings an animal or bird. Aaron's sons, the priests, are spoken of in the third person as the ones who handle the blood, the altar and the fire.
settings.when: At Mount Sinai, in the first month of the second year after the exodus, just after the tent of meeting was set up (Exodus 40:17)
settings.why: The tent is built and God's glory has filled it. The problem is how ordinary people may now come near. This law tells the lay worshiper what to bring and where to bring it: the entrance of the tent of meeting. He leans his hand on the animal and slaughters it himself. It allows cattle, sheep or birds, so that the poor can come too. Because it is spoken to lay people, it reads as a worshiper's guide; the priests' own manual comes later (6:8–7:38).
views: Traditional readers: given through Moses at Sinai, as the book says. Critical scholars: priestly law. Some date it to the First Temple (Kaufmann, Haran, Milgrom), others to the exile or after (Wellhausen). Many of the rites are older than the writing. The same view applies to chapters 1–16.

title: Flour, Oil and Salt
sum: The second offering is the grain offering, the one anyone could afford: fine flour with oil and frankincense, raw or baked in an oven, on a griddle or in a pan. A handful, the "token portion," goes up in smoke; the rest is a most holy share for the priests. No yeast or honey may go on the altar, but every offering must be seasoned with salt, "the salt of your God's covenant." The chapter ends with the roasted first grain of the harvest.

Where chapter 1 was about blood and fire, chapter 2 is about the kitchen. It brings the farmer's daily bread to God's table, and the rabbis heard in its opening word, "a soul," God saying that the poor man who brings flour offers his very life.

views.H: The everyday offering of an agricultural people, given in the wilderness for life in the land. Its variety of breads reflects real Israelite cooking.
views.C: A Priestly classification of a wide range of older grain offerings. Some scholars think the "token portion" reflects a move from feeding God to a token offering.
views.A: Salt (lasting), yeast and honey (fermenting): the chapter sorts substances by whether they preserve or decay, matching the book's concern with life and death.
views.J: The rabbis read 2:1 as God valuing the poor man's flour as his soul (Menachot 104b). Salt on the Sabbath bread today recalls the salt on the altar.
views.X: Jesus' sayings on salt (Mark 9:49–50; Matthew 5:13) and yeast (Matthew 16:6; 1 Corinthians 5:6–8) draw on this chapter's symbols. Cornelius's prayers rise as a "memorial" (Acts 10:4).

echoes: Genesis 4:3–5; Numbers 15:1–10; Numbers 18:19; 2 Chronicles 13:5; Malachi 1:11; Mark 9:49–50; Matthew 5:13; Acts 10:4; Philippians 4:18

settings.what: The law of the grain offering
settings.to: The Israelites who bring offerings; the priests, Aaron's sons, receive the token portion and eat the rest
settings.when: Continuing the speech from the tent of meeting at Sinai
settings.why: To set out a gift of flour, oil and incense that anyone could bring, cooked or raw. Yeast and honey may not go on the altar, but salt must. It also tells the priests' share: what is left belongs to Aaron and his sons as most holy. The rules about firstfruits (2:12–16) look ahead to harvests.

title: A Meal Shared with God
sum: The peace offering is the one ordinary Israelites ate. A male or female from the cattle, sheep or goats is offered; its fat, the kidneys and the lobe of the liver go up in smoke as "food" for God, and, as chapter 7 will explain, the priests and the worshiper's family share the meat. The chapter ends with a rule for all time: no fat and no blood may be eaten.

The peace offering turns sacrifice into a feast. God receives the best part, the priests their share, and the family celebrates before him. It is the background of many biblical meals before God, from the covenant meal on Sinai to the Passover and the Lord's Supper.

views.H: The festive offering of Israel's life, behind the meals of Elkanah's family at Shiloh (1 Samuel 1) and Solomon's dedication (1 Kings 8:63).
views.C: An ancient type of sacrifice, close to the Ugaritic and Punic "peace" or "well-being" offerings, regulated here by the Priestly writers. Deuteronomy 12 later centralizes all such meals at one sanctuary.
views.A: A communion meal in Robertson Smith's sense: God, priests and people share one animal. The fat and blood are reserved as God's share of life.
views.J: The rabbis said the shelamim bring peace to the world because everyone gets a portion (Rashi). The ban on chelev fat and blood remains part of kashrut.
views.X: Christians see the shared sacrificial meal behind the Lord's Supper (1 Corinthians 10:16–21) and "peace" with God through Christ's blood (Colossians 1:20; Ephesians 2:13–14).

echoes: Exodus 24:5–11; Genesis 9:4; 1 Samuel 1:3–5; 1 Samuel 2:15–17; 1 Kings 8:63; Psalm 50:12–14; Acts 15:20; 1 Corinthians 10:16–21

settings.what: The law of the peace offering
settings.to: The Israelites who bring a peace offering from the herd or flock; the priests who burn the fat on the altar
settings.when: Continuing the speech from the tent of meeting at Sinai
settings.why: To show how an Israelite can share a meal with God. The fat and inner parts go up in smoke, and the worshiper eats the rest. It ends with a rule for all Israel in all their homes: eat no fat and no blood (3:17). The problem it answers is how to eat meat in a way that honors the life God gave.

title: When Anyone Sins by Mistake
sum: A new kind of offering begins: the sin offering, for wrongs done by mistake. The law climbs down the social ladder: the anointed high priest, the whole community, a leader, an ordinary person. For the high priest and the community, the blood is carried into the tent, spattered seven times before the veil and put on the incense altar, and the bull is burned outside the camp. For a leader or commoner, the blood touches the horns of the outer altar and the priest eats the meat. Each section ends: "the priest will make atonement ... and he will be forgiven."
The chapter takes accidental sin seriously. Even the highest leader errs, and his error pollutes God's house more deeply than anyone's.

views.H: The core of Israel's system of atonement, carried out at the tabernacle and temple until AD 70.
views.C: Many critical scholars see the hatta't as a later development of the Priestly system, absent from older lists of offerings (Exodus 20:24) and prominent in Ezekiel (Ezekiel 43–45).
views.A: Milgrom's model: sin, like impurity, pollutes the sanctuary at different depths depending on who sinned, and the blood cleans it at the matching place.
views.J: The rabbis read the leader's "when" as "happy" (Horayot 10b) and built the tractate Horayot on errors of the court and the high priest.
views.X: Paul's "for sin" (Romans 8:3) and Hebrews' bodies burned outside the camp (Hebrews 13:11–12) draw on this chapter. Many Christians see Christ as the sin offering who purifies both people and heavenly sanctuary.

deep.b:
Jacob Milgrom (1976, 1991) argued that the hatta't does not cleanse the sinner at all. Sin and impurity give off a kind of pollution that clings to the sanctuary, deeper the graver the sin: ordinary sins to the outer altar, the high priest's or the nation's to the tent, deliberate rebellions to the inner room. The blood of the offering works like a ritual detergent, put on the place that is soiled. The sinner is cleansed by his remorse, and the sanctuary by the blood; once a year, on the Day of Atonement, the whole building is scrubbed (16:16). If the pollution builds up unchecked, God will leave, as Ezekiel saw (Ezekiel 10).

Critics have pushed back on several points. N. Kiuchi and Jay Sklar note that the text says atonement is made "for him," from "his sin" (4:26), so the person, not just the building, is affected. Roy Gane proposes two stages: individual offerings during the year purge the offerer and transfer the evil to the sanctuary; the Day of Atonement removes it from the sanctuary. Hyam Maccoby questions whether sin "pollutes" from a distance at all. Jonathan Klawans accepts that grave sins defile the sanctuary and the land without contact (20:3; 18:24–28), but argues that Milgrom blurs two systems: ritual impurity, which is contagious and washable, and moral impurity, which is neither. Most agree with Milgrom that the offering is about purification as well as forgiveness, which is why many now call it the "purification offering."

echoes: Numbers 15:22–31; Psalm 19:12–13; Ezekiel 45:18–20; Hosea 4:6–9; Romans 8:3; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Hebrews 9:7; Hebrews 13:11–13

settings.what: The law of the sin offering
settings.to: The Israelites (4:2). The cases are ranked by who has sinned. They cover the anointed priest, the whole community, a leader, or any ordinary person. 5:1–13 covers failing to testify, touching something unclean and careless oaths.
settings.when: At Sinai, in the camp around the tent of meeting
settings.why: To deal with sins done by mistake and with failures that a person later realizes. For the high priest and the whole community the blood is taken inside the tent. For a leader or an ordinary person it goes on the outer altar. The sliding scale in 5:7–13 lets the poor bring birds or flour. The problem is not only the person's guilt but the harm done to the sanctuary where God lives.
views: Milgrom: the 'purification offering' cleans the sanctuary, which Israel's sins and impurities have polluted. Gane, Sklar and Kiuchi: it also cleanses and ransoms the person who brings it.

title: Silence, Touch and Careless Words
sum: Chapter 5 finishes the sin offering with some everyday cases: a witness who keeps quiet under a public curse, a person who forgets he touched something unclean, someone who blurts out an oath and forgets it. When he realizes it, he must confess and bring an offering scaled to his means: a lamb or goat, two birds, or even a little flour. Then comes the guilt offering, a ram for sacrilege against holy things, with repayment plus a fifth, and for wrongs a person may have done without knowing.
The chapter is about conscience. Many of these sins are hidden even from the sinner, and the remedy begins with words: "he is to confess."

views.H: Practical law for real cases in Israel's courts and sanctuary.
views.C: Scholars note that 5:1–13 seems to stand between chapter 4 and the guilt offering, and may join two originally separate laws; the word asham is used in both senses.
views.A: Hidden guilt, forgotten contact, broken words: the chapter maps invisible boundaries that a person can cross without seeing them.
views.J: The rabbis built the "suspended" guilt offering for doubtful sins on 5:17, and Maimonides drew the duty of spoken confession from this and Numbers 5:7.
views.X: Christians read Isaiah 53:10, the servant's life made an asham, as fulfilled in Christ, and the call to confess in 1 John 1:9.

echoes: Numbers 5:5–8; Judges 17:1–2; Ecclesiastes 5:2–6; Isaiah 53:10; Matthew 5:33–37; Luke 2:24; Hebrews 9:22; 1 John 1:9

settings.what: The law of the guilt offering
settings.to: Spoken to Moses (5:14; 6:1). No hearers are named. The law concerns any Israelite who has wronged the LORD's holy things or cheated a neighbor.
settings.when: At Sinai, in the camp around the tent of meeting
settings.why: To make wrongs right in two ways at once. The wrongdoer repays what was taken, plus a fifth, and brings a ram to the priest. 6:1–7 treats cheating a neighbor as unfaithfulness to the LORD himself. The problem is how someone who lied under oath, or kept what was not his, can come back.
views: Milgrom: because these wrongs (6:2–5) are deliberate, the law shows that confession and repayment can turn them into wrongs the altar can deal with. Others read them simply as a separate class of offense.

title: The Fire That Must Not Go Out
sum: Two units meet here. Verses 1–7 finish the guilt offering: a person who cheats a neighbor and lies under oath has wronged God, and must repay in full, add a fifth, and then bring a ram. From 6:8 the book turns to the priests, going back over the offerings from their side. The fire on the altar must burn all night and never go out; the priest in linen removes the ashes. The grain offering is eaten by priests in the holy place; the priests' own grain offering is burned whole; the sin offering is eaten by the priest who offers it, and whatever touches it becomes holy.
It is a manual for clergy, but it carries a moral line through it: wronging a neighbor is breaking faith with God, and repair comes before ritual.

views.H: The priests' manual for the tabernacle service, kept up in the temple.
views.C: Chapters 6–7 are a separate collection of priestly instructions (torot), each with its own heading, joined to the lay manual of 1–5.
views.A: The perpetual fire marks the altar as a living center; the ash rite shows that even holy waste needs ritual handling.
views.J: The Torah portion Tzav begins at 6:8. Rabbis read the ever-burning fire as the fire of Torah study and prayer in the heart.
views.X: Matthew 5:23–24 (reconcile before offering) echoes 6:1–7, and Hebrews 13:10 builds on the rule that blood-carried sin offerings were not eaten.

echoes: Numbers 5:5–8; Psalm 51:4; Haggai 2:11–13; Ezekiel 44:19; Matthew 5:23–24; Luke 19:8; Romans 12:11; Hebrews 13:10–13

settings.what: The priests' instructions for the offerings
settings.to: Aaron and his sons, the priests (6:9; 6:25)
settings.when: At Sinai, before the priests began to serve
settings.why: This section is for the priests alone. It goes over the same offerings again from the priest's side. The priests keep the altar fire burning, wear linen and eat the most holy portions in a holy place. The high priest offers a daily grain offering (6:19–23). It answers practical questions: what the priests may eat, where, and how long. Knowing that the priests are the hearers explains why it repeats chapters 1–5 in a new order.

title: Thanks, Vows and the Priests' Share
sum: The priests' manual continues with the guilt offering and with what the priests may keep: the hide of a burnt offering, cooked grain offerings, the meat of sin and guilt offerings. The peace offering has three kinds: thanks, a vow, or a freewill gift. Thank offerings must be eaten the same day, the others by the second; leftovers are burned on the third. No one unclean may eat holy meat. Fat and blood are never to be eaten. The breast and right thigh go to the priests. A summary closes the whole first section of the book, "which the LORD commanded Moses on Mount Sinai."
The chapter shows sacrifice as Israel's economy of joy: rescued people bring thanks, families feast, priests are fed.

views.H: The rules that kept sanctuary meals holy and supported the priesthood.
views.C: A priestly collection that likely reflects the practice of a central sanctuary. The conflict between "Sinai" (7:38) and "the tent" (1:1) may show two layers.
views.A: Time limits on eating, and the ban on eating while unclean, keep the holy and the unclean from meeting at the table.
views.J: The rabbis taught that the thank offering will remain in the age to come, and that studying these laws counts as offering them (Menachot 110a).
views.X: The "sacrifice of praise" (Hebrews 13:15) and Paul's defense of supporting ministers (1 Corinthians 9:13) draw on this chapter.

echoes: Psalm 50:14; Psalm 107:22; Psalm 116:17–19; Proverbs 7:14; Hosea 14:2; Acts 21:23–26; 1 Corinthians 9:13; Hebrews 13:15

settings.what: Fat, blood and the priests' share
settings.to: The Israelites (7:23; 7:29), every household that eats meat or brings a peace offering
settings.when: At Sinai; the closing words (7:37–38) mark the end of the offering laws given on Mount Sinai
settings.why: To bind every Israelite, not only the priests. No one may eat the fat of cattle, sheep or goats, or any blood. The breast and the thigh of each peace offering go to Aaron and his sons. It answers how the priests are to be fed: the people give part of their own meal.

title: Seven Days at the Door
sum: Moses now does what God commanded in Exodus 29. Before the whole community he washes Aaron and his sons, dresses Aaron in the high priest's garments, anoints the tabernacle, the altar and Aaron himself, and dresses his sons. A bull is offered as a sin offering to purify the altar, a ram as a burnt offering, and a second ram, the ram of ordination, whose blood touches the right ear, thumb and big toe of each new priest. Oil and blood are spattered on them and their clothes. For seven days they must stay at the entrance of the tent.
Again and again the chapter says, "just as the LORD commanded Moses." It is a picture of perfect obedience, and it sets up the shock of chapter 10.

views.H: The historical founding of Israel's priesthood at Sinai, with Moses acting as priest for the occasion.
views.C: A fulfillment report built from Exodus 29 and 40, giving the Aaronic priests of later times their charter.
views.A: A textbook rite of passage: separation (washing, dressing), a liminal week at the threshold, and incorporation on the eighth day.
views.J: The rabbis said Moses served in a white robe without a hem during these seven days (Avodah Zarah 34a), and that "the small held the many" at the doorway.
views.X: Hebrews contrasts priests "appointed" in weakness with "a Son made perfect forever" (Hebrews 7:28), using the Greek word for ordination. 1 Peter 2:9 calls the church a royal priesthood.

echoes: Exodus 28:1–43; Exodus 29:1–37; Exodus 40:9–16; Psalm 133:2; Psalm 99:6; Hebrews 5:1–5; Hebrews 7:28; 1 Peter 2:9; Revelation 1:6

settings.what: The ordination of Aaron and his sons
settings.by: The LORD's command, carried out by Moses
settings.to: Spoken to Moses (8:1). Moses then speaks to the whole community gathered at the entrance of the tent of meeting (8:5). Aaron and his sons are the ones ordained.
settings.when: At Sinai, over seven days, carrying out what the LORD had ordered in Exodus 29
settings.why: To make Aaron and his sons priests in public. Then all Israel would know who may come near the altar. Moses acts as priest this once. The repeated words 'as the LORD commanded Moses' show that the priesthood rests on God's word, not on Aaron's claim.

settings.what: Moses' charge for the seven days
settings.to: Aaron and his sons
settings.when: At the end of the first day of ordination
settings.why: To keep the new priests at the entrance of the tent for seven days, eating the ordination meal there. If they leave, they will die. The charge warns that coming near God is dangerous, which the next chapters will show.

title: The Glory Appears
sum: On the eighth day Aaron begins. He offers a calf as a sin offering and a ram as a burnt offering for himself, then the people's goat, calf, lamb, ox and ram, and their grain offering. He lifts his hands and blesses the people. Moses and Aaron go into the tent, come out and bless them again, and the glory of the LORD appears to all. Fire comes out from before the LORD and eats up the offering on the altar. The people shout for joy and fall on their faces.

This is the high point of the book's first half. All the building in Exodus and all the instructions in Leviticus 1–8 have led to this moment: God accepts Israel's worship and shows himself. The next verse turns joy into grief.

views.H: The inauguration of public worship at the tabernacle, in the first month of the second year after the exodus (Exodus 40:17).
views.C: A climactic scene of the Priestly narrative, matching the glory at Sinai (Exodus 24:16–17) and the filling of the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34). Some scholars see this, not Exodus 40, as P's original culmination.
views.A: The eighth day completes the rite of passage of chapter 8: the new priests act, and the community receives their blessing.
views.J: The rabbis said the day "took ten crowns" (Shabbat 87b) and that Aaron's calf answered the golden calf (Sifra). The priestly blessing is still spoken in synagogues with raised hands.
views.X: Hebrews notes the high priest offered first for himself (Hebrews 7:27). Luke ends his Gospel with Jesus lifting his hands to bless (Luke 24:50–51).

echoes: Exodus 24:16–17; Exodus 40:34–35; Numbers 6:22–27; Judges 6:21; 1 Kings 8:10–11; 1 Kings 18:38–39; 2 Chronicles 7:1–3; Luke 24:50–53; Hebrews 7:27

settings.what: Moses' orders for the eighth day
settings.to: Aaron, his sons and the elders of Israel (9:1), and through Aaron all the Israelites (9:3)
settings.when: The eighth day, the first day the priests serve
settings.why: To set up the first public offerings, first for Aaron and then for the people. They come with a promise: today the LORD will appear to you. The purpose is to show that the new priesthood works.

settings.what: Aaron's blessing
settings.by: Aaron, then Moses and Aaron together
settings.to: All the people gathered before the tent
settings.when: After the first offerings, as Aaron came down from the altar
settings.why: To bless the people, perhaps with words like those of Numbers 6:24–26. The blessing is answered by the glory of the LORD and fire from before him. The people shout and fall on their faces: God has accepted the worship.
views: Many interpreters, Jewish and Christian, think Aaron used the priestly blessing later given in Numbers 6:24–26; the text does not say.

title: Strange Fire
sum: On that same day Aaron's two oldest sons, Nadab and Abihu, take their fire pans, put fire and incense in them, and bring "strange fire" before the LORD, "which he had not commanded them." Fire from the LORD eats them up. Moses quotes God: "In those who come near me I will show myself holy." Aaron is silent. Cousins carry the bodies out; Aaron and his surviving sons may not mourn. God then speaks to Aaron alone: no wine on duty, and the priests must separate holy from ordinary and unclean from clean, and teach Israel. The chapter ends with Moses angry that the priests did not eat the people's sin offering, and Aaron's quiet answer, which Moses accepts.

Leviticus is mostly law, but at its center stands this story of sudden death. It teaches by shock what the laws teach by rule: the holy is life-giving but dangerous, and closeness to God raises the stakes.
readings: Read as a warning

The priests improvised in worship, and God's holiness destroyed them. Most Jewish and Christian readers take it this way, with parallels in Uzzah (2 Samuel 6:6–7) and Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5:1–11).
Read as a mystery
Some modern readers, such as Edward Greenstein, stress that the text gives no motive, and that the story shows how close the holy is to death. Aaron's silence is the right response.
Read as zeal
Philo and some rabbis honored Nadab and Abihu as men consumed by love of God, "greater than Moses and Aaron" in Rashi's telling (10:3).

views.H: A real event on the day of inauguration, recorded to warn later priests.
views.C: Some critics see a polemic against a rival priestly group, or against incense rites outside the official system (compare Korah, Numbers 16). Others see a story placed to explain the law of 16:1–2.
views.A: The fire that accepted the offering (9:24) consumes the improvisers (10:2): the book's boundaries between holy and common are shown to be life and death.
views.J: The rabbis gave many reasons for the deaths (Leviticus Rabbah 20; Sifra) and praised Aaron's silence. On Yom Kippur the death of the righteous is said to atone, and this chapter's reading is linked to that day.
views.X: Christian writers read it alongside Hebrews 12:28–29: serve God "with reverence and fear, for our God is a consuming fire."

deep.b:
The text says only that the fire was "strange" and "not commanded." Later readers filled the gap with at least a dozen reasons. The rabbis list: they were drunk (from 10:9); they went in without washing hands and feet, or without the full priestly garments; they had no children; they never married, thinking no woman good enough; they gave a ruling in front of Moses their teacher; they said, "When will these two old men die so that we can lead the people?" (Sifra; Leviticus Rabbah 20:6–10; Eruvin 63a; Sanhedrin 52a). Modern scholars usually point to the fire itself, coals not taken from the altar (compare 16:12), or to incense offered at the wrong time or place.

The story's own placement suggests the point. It follows seven repetitions of "just as the LORD commanded" (chapter 8) and stands as their opposite: "which he had not commanded them."

deep.title: Claude's theory: the brothers and the calf
deep.b: This is my own suggestion. Nadab and Abihu's sin echoes their father's. At the golden calf Aaron made a festival "for the LORD" (Exodus 32:5) by his own design; here his sons bring fire to the LORD by their own design. In both cases the worship is aimed at the right God but shaped by human initiative. Leviticus 9 has Aaron atone with a calf for himself (9:2); chapter 10 then shows the next generation repeating the pattern in a new form, and God's response is immediate. If this is right, the chapter warns that the danger in worship is not only false gods but self-made ways to the true one. The rabbis made related links: the Sifra on 9:2 ties Aaron's calf offering to the golden calf, and Rashi on Deuteronomy 9:20 reads God's anger "to destroy" Aaron as the death of his sons, because of the calf (compare Leviticus Rabbah 10:5). Exodus 32:25–29 already ties the calf to the Levites' ordination, so the idea overlaps published readings; the specific pairing of 10:1 with Exodus 32:5 is mine.

echoes: Exodus 6:23; Exodus 24:1; Exodus 24:9–11; Exodus 30:9; Numbers 3:4; Numbers 16:35; 2 Samuel 6:6–7; Ezekiel 22:26; Ezekiel 44:21–23; Malachi 2:7; Acts 5:1–11; Hebrews 12:28–29

settings.what: The LORD's word about those who come near
settings.to: Aaron, just after the deaths of Nadab and Abihu
settings.when: The same day the glory appeared, after the strange fire
settings.why: To explain the deaths: God shows himself holy in those who come near him. The saying is for the priests above all. Aaron's silence is his answer.

settings.what: Orders on mourning
settings.to: Aaron and his sons Eleazar and Ithamar
settings.when: Right after the deaths, while the bodies are carried out
settings.why: To keep the anointed priests at their post. They must not mourn in public or leave the tent, but the whole house of Israel may weep. It answers a hard question: how can priests grieve and still serve?

settings.what: The LORD's rule for priests: no wine, and teach
settings.by: The LORD, speaking to Aaron directly
settings.to: Aaron and his sons, for all their generations
settings.when: The only time in Leviticus the LORD speaks to Aaron alone
settings.why: To forbid wine and beer when the priests go into the tent. It also gives them a double job. They separate the holy from the ordinary and the unclean from the clean, and they teach the Israelites. Many readers link the rule to the deaths just told. The verse also sets out the plan of chapters 11–15.

settings.what: The dispute over the sin offering
settings.to: Aaron and his remaining sons, Eleazar and Ithamar
settings.when: Later that same day
settings.why: Moses insists on the rules for eating the priests' portions. He is angry that the goat was burned, not eaten. Aaron replies that eating it on such a day would not please the LORD, and Moses is satisfied. The exchange shows priests applying the law with judgment, not only by rote.
views: Rabbinic readers: as a mourner Aaron could not eat holy food that day. Milgrom: the sin had polluted the inner sanctuary, so the offering had to be burned.

title: What You May Eat
sum: The laws of clean and unclean begin with food. Land animals must both chew the cud and have a split hoof; the camel, hyrax, hare and pig fail. Water creatures need fins and scales. Some twenty birds are forbidden, mostly birds of prey and carrion-eaters. Of winged insects only locusts and their kin are allowed. Then come rules for touching dead animals, including small creatures like mice and lizards, which make pots, clothes and food unclean. The chapter ends with its reason: "Be holy, for I am holy."

For Jews this chapter is the foundation of kashrut; for Christians it raises the question of what Jesus and the apostles changed. For every reader it shows a God who cares about the ordinary act of eating.
readings: Read as symbol
Mary Douglas: clean animals fit their category, unclean ones blur the lines, and the table becomes a map of an ordered world, matching Genesis 1's "each by its kind."
Read as identity and discipline
The laws make Israel distinct (20:24–26); the rabbis call them decrees obeyed out of love, not because pork is bad.
Read as fulfilled
Christians, following Mark 7:19 and Acts 10, read the separation of foods as a picture of Israel's separation from the nations, ended when Gentiles were welcomed.

views.H: Food laws given at Sinai and kept by Israel ever since, with Deuteronomy 14 as a parallel.
views.C: Leviticus 11 and Deuteronomy 14 share an older list; Leviticus adds the rules on carcasses and the holiness ending, likely from the Holiness writers (11:43–45).
views.A: Douglas's classic reading in Purity and Danger (1966), revised in Leviticus as Literature (1999), where she argued the laws protect the vulnerable creatures God made.
views.J: The heart of kashrut, expanded in the Talmud's tractate Chullin. The Sifra's teaching: do not say "I hate pork," but "I would like it, but my Father in heaven has forbidden it."
views.X: Most churches hold that Christ made "all foods clean" (Mark 7:19; Acts 10; Romans 14). Some Messianic Jewish and Adventist Christians keep the clean-animal distinctions.

deep.b:
Hygiene. From Maimonides (Guide 3.48) to modern popular writers, some argue the forbidden animals are less healthy. Critics answer that the text never says so, that many allowed foods carry disease, and that the New Testament's freedom would then be dangerous.

Symbol and order. Mary Douglas argued that holiness means wholeness and order. Clean animals are "proper" members of their realm; animals that cross categories (sea creatures without scales, four-footed swarming things) are unclean. Critics found her system incomplete; Douglas herself revised it.

Ethics. The Letter of Aristeas (second century BC) and Philo read the birds of prey as teaching Israel not to be violent, and the cud-chewers as teaching memory and meditation. The Epistle of Barnabas (chapter 10) read the same laws as moral allegory for Christians.

Reverence for life. Jacob Milgrom argued that the system, with the ban on blood (17:11), limits Israel's killing to a few kinds of animal and teaches that life belongs to God.

Analogy. Gordon Wenham, building on Douglas, saw three ranks of animals (unclean, clean, fit for the altar) matching three ranks of people (the nations, Israel, the priests). Douglas developed the idea in Leviticus as Literature.

Identity. Leviticus 20:24–26 links clean food to Israel's separation from the nations. Archaeology shows pork avoidance as an early marker (see 11:7).

Decree. The rabbis class these laws as chukkim, statutes whose reason is not given, to be obeyed as an act of love and loyalty (Sifra on 20:26; Rashi on 19:19).

echoes: Genesis 1:20–25; Genesis 7:2; Genesis 9:3–4; Deuteronomy 14:3–21; Daniel 1:8; 2 Maccabees 6:18–31; Mark 7:14–23; Acts 10:9–16; Acts 15:20; Romans 14:14–20; 1 Peter 1:15–16

settings.what: The laws of clean and unclean animals
settings.by: The LORD, speaking to Moses and Aaron
settings.to: The Israelites (11:2): every household that eats, hunts, fishes or handles dead animals. Moses and Aaron are to teach it.
settings.when: At Sinai, for life in the camp and afterward
settings.why: To tell every Israelite which land animals, water creatures, birds and swarming things may be eaten. It also says that touching a carcass makes a person unclean until evening. It ends with the reason: be holy, for I am holy (11:44–45). The food laws were meant for daily life in the home, not only at the sanctuary. So they mark Israel off at every meal.
views: Readers have explained the lists in several ways. Maimonides pointed in part to health, and the Letter of Aristeas to symbols of virtue. Douglas pointed to order and category, and Milgrom to what was offered on the altar. Many say the reasons are not given and the point is obedience.
Knohl and Milgrom: the closing call to holiness was added by the Holiness school.

traditions.q: Should Christians still keep the food laws of Leviticus 11?
views: No. Jesus declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19; Catechism 582), and the Council of Florence (1442) taught that the food distinctions of the law ended with the gospel. Fasting and abstaining from meat on certain days are church discipline, not purity laws.

The food laws of Moses have ended, but the Orthodox fast from meat, dairy, and often fish, wine and oil on many days of the year. They see these fasts as training in self-control, not as rules of clean and unclean.

The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, one of the Oriental Orthodox churches, keeps the ban on pork and other animals listed as unclean. It treats this as an inherited practice of the church, not as a condition of salvation. Other Oriental Orthodox churches, such as the Armenian Apostolic Church, do not keep these food laws.

The ceremonial laws, including the food laws, pointed ahead to Christ and are now abolished (Westminster Confession 19.3). Peter's vision (Acts 10) and Paul's teaching (Romans 14) show that no food is unclean in itself.

Adventists avoid the meats that Leviticus 11 calls unclean, because the distinction is older than Moses (Genesis 7:2) and serves health and holiness. Many also go further and avoid meat, alcohol and tobacco (Fundamental Beliefs 22).

title: After a Birth
sum: Eight verses on childbirth. A mother is unclean seven days after a boy, like her monthly flow, and the boy is circumcised on the eighth day; then for thirty-three days she may not touch holy things or enter the sanctuary. After a girl the periods double: fourteen days and sixty-six. At the end she brings a lamb for a burnt offering and a bird for a sin offering, or two birds if she is poor, and the priest makes atonement, "and she will be clean."

This short chapter has drawn some of the hardest questions about Leviticus. It is honest to say both that birth is not called sinful and that the text treats sons and daughters differently without explaining why.

views.H: Laws for Israelite mothers kept at the sanctuary; Luke 2:22–24 shows Mary and Joseph keeping them.
views.C: Comparable rules from Hittite, Greek and other cultures prescribe set periods of impurity after birth, sometimes longer for girls; the Priestly writers adapted a widespread custom.
views.A: Birth, like death, is a boundary of life; the blood of birth is life leaving the body, so the mother is set apart until the flow ends.
views.J: The Talmud's explanation of the offering (the oath of labor, Niddah 31b), and the later law of the mother's immersion. The portion Tazria is named from 12:2.
views.X: Luke 2:22–24 (Mary's purification) and the feast of the Presentation (Candlemas). The Lamb of God's mother could not afford a lamb.

deep.b: Two things are true. First, the text does not say that birth, sex or women are sinful. Uncleanness here is a ritual state, shared by men with discharges (chapter 15) and anyone who touches a corpse, and the mother's "sin offering" is a purification rite (see 4:3). Children are a blessing (Genesis 1:28; Psalm 127:3). Second, the law doubles the time after a daughter and gives no reason, and readers who see in this the inequality of an ancient patriarchal society are reading the text, not inventing a problem. Jewish and Christian interpreters have answered in different ways: some explain the difference (12:5), some treat the law as for its time, some reject parts of it. A fair reading holds both points together.

echoes: Genesis 3:16; Genesis 17:10–14; Psalm 127:3; Luke 1:59; Luke 2:21–24; John 7:22–23; Galatians 4:4

settings.what: The law after childbirth
settings.to: The Israelites (12:2), and in particular every mother after giving birth, with her household
settings.when: At Sinai, for life in the camp
settings.why: To set the days of a mother's uncleanness and the offerings that end it. She brings a lamb and a bird, or two birds if she is poor (12:8). Birth brings no sin, but it brings blood and the edge of life and death, which must be kept away from the holy. The law tells the mother when she may again touch holy things.
views: Milgrom: it purifies the sanctuary, not the mother's character. Readers differ on the double time for a girl. Some see protection in it, others a mark of lower status.

traditions.q: Mary brought the offering of 12:8 after Jesus' birth (Luke 2:22–24). Did she need cleansing from sin?
views: No. Mary was kept free from original sin from her conception (Ineffabilis Deus, 1854; Catechism 491) and committed no personal sin (Catechism 493). Aquinas taught that she kept this law out of humility and obedience, as her Son was circumcised and later baptized without needing it.

Mary is the all-holy one, free from personal sin, but the Orthodox do not accept the 1854 dogma; she shared the mortality of all Adam's children. The feast on February 2, the Meeting of the Lord, centers on Christ meeting Simeon in the temple.

Mary was a believer saved by grace like everyone else, who called God her Savior (Luke 1:47). Reformed writers often note that 12:6–8 calls for a sin offering and see no reason to make her an exception, while honoring her faith.
Mary was a godly woman chosen for a unique role, but only Christ was without sin. Her offering of birds shows both the family's poverty and her place among sinners who needed the Savior she bore.

title: The Priest Looks at the Skin
sum: The longest chapter in Leviticus teaches priests to examine marks on the skin: swellings, flaking, bright spots, raw flesh, boils, burns, scaly patches on the head and beard. White hair and depth below the skin are warning signs; a doubtful case is shut away for seven days and looked at again. The person declared unclean must tear his clothes, let his hair loose, cover his lip, call "Unclean! Unclean!" and live alone outside the camp. The chapter ends with the same kind of mark in wool, linen and leather.
The disease here is not leprosy as we know it. What matters to Leviticus is not cure but status: whether the person can live among the people and come near God's house.

views.H: Diagnostic law for a real class of skin conditions, applied by priests in Israel.
views.C: An old body of priestly lore on skin conditions, comparable to Mesopotamian omen and medical texts, organized by the Priestly writers.
views.A: The diseased skin looks like a body wasting toward death; the rite treats the person as a mourner, and his return (chapter 14) as a rebirth.
views.J: The rabbis taught that tsara'at punished slander (lashon hara) and stinginess (Arakhin 15b–16a). The tractate Negaim works out the details.
views.X: Jesus touches and heals men with skin disease and sends them to the priests (Mark 1:40–44; Luke 17:11–19). Preachers long used the disease as a picture of sin.

deep.b: The Hebrew tsara'at became Greek lepra, Latin lepra and English "leprosy," and from the Middle Ages on it was identified with Hansen's disease, a bacterial infection that damages nerves. Lepers were shut out of towns in Europe partly because of these chapters. But the symptoms in Leviticus do not match Hansen's disease: there is no numbness, no loss of fingers or toes, and some cases clear up in a week. The same word is used for cloth and walls. Most scholars, including E. V. Hulse and Jacob Milgrom, conclude that tsara'at covered several scaly or flaking conditions, perhaps including psoriasis and fungal infections. Modern translations use "skin disease" or "scale disease" to avoid adding stigma to people with Hansen's disease, a stigma the Bible itself did not intend.

echoes: Exodus 4:6–7; Numbers 5:2–4; Numbers 12:10–15; Deuteronomy 24:8–9; 2 Kings 5:1–27; 2 Kings 7:3–10; 2 Kings 15:5; 2 Chronicles 26:19–21; Mark 1:40–45; Luke 17:11–19

settings.what: The priest's examination of skin disease and mold
settings.by: The LORD, speaking to Moses and Aaron
settings.to: Spoken to Moses and Aaron (13:1). There is no 'speak to the Israelites'. It is the priests' procedure: the priest is spoken of in the third person (13:2). The person with the mark must live outside the camp while unclean (13:45–46).
settings.when: At Sinai, for the camp around the tent
settings.why: To give priests a way to judge a skin mark. The priest looks, waits seven days, looks again, and declares the person clean or unclean. It answers who may live inside the camp, near the tent, and who must stay outside. The priest acts as a judge of status, not as a doctor who heals. 13:47–59 applies the same test to cloth.
views: Hulse and most scholars: not Hansen's disease (leprosy) but various skin conditions. Baden and Moss stress that the concern is ritual status, not medicine.

title: Coming Back from Outside
sum: When the skin disease is healed, the priest goes out to the person outside the camp. One bird is killed over living water; the other, dipped in its blood with cedar, scarlet yarn and hyssop, is set free over the open field. The person washes, shaves and waits seven days, then shaves all his hair again. On the eighth day he brings a guilt offering, a sin offering, a burnt offering and a grain offering; blood and oil are put on his right ear, thumb and toe, as on a priest. A simpler rite is given for the poor. The chapter ends with mold in a house: inspection, removal of stones, replastering, and if all fails, demolition, with the same rite of the two birds for a house made clean.
The chapter turns an outcast into a member again, step by step, with honors usually given to priests.

views.H: The rite by which healed Israelites returned to camp and sanctuary; Jesus told the men he healed to keep it.
views.C: Two rites seem joined: an old elimination ritual with the birds (14:2–8), and a sanctuary ritual on the eighth day (14:10–32). The house law looks to settled life in Canaan.
views.A: A rebirth in stages, outside to camp to tent to sanctuary; the shaving makes him like a newborn, the blood on his extremities marks a new beginning.
views.J: Rashi's midrash: the house plague revealed hidden Canaanite treasure. The rabbis also taught that a house with tsara'at may never have existed and the law is for study.
views.X: Mark 1:44 and Luke 17:14: Jesus sends the healed to the priests. Some fathers read the two birds as Christ dying and rising.

deep.title: Claude's theory: three eighth days
deep.b: This is my own suggestion, though it builds on Mary Douglas and Jacob Milgrom. Leviticus puts an "eighth day" at three crossings: the priests begin service on the eighth day after a week at the door (8:33–9:1); a baby boy is circumcised on the eighth day (12:3); the healed person and the person cleansed from a discharge come before the LORD on the eighth day (14:10; 15:14). The same blood on ear, thumb and toe links the priest (8:23) and the healed outcast (14:14). I suggest the book deliberately presents these three as one pattern: ordination, birth into the covenant and return from death are all "new creation" after a completed week, each beginning on the day after the seventh, as Israel's whole worship begins on the eighth day of chapter 9. If so, Leviticus treats the poorest outcast's return as a kind of ordination into the people of priests (Exodus 19:6).

echoes: Numbers 19:1–22; Psalm 51:7; 2 Kings 5:14; Jeremiah 2:13; John 4:10–14; Mark 1:44; Luke 17:14; Hebrews 9:13–14

settings.what: The rite for a person made clean
settings.to: Spoken to Moses (14:1). No hearers are named. The law concerns the priest, who goes outside the camp, and the person who has healed (14:2–3).
settings.when: At Sinai, for the camp
settings.why: To bring a healed person back step by step. First comes a rite with two birds outside the camp, with washing and shaving. After seven days there are offerings at the tent on the eighth day. It answers how one who was shut out may come home. A poor person may bring less (14:21–32).

settings.what: The law of mold in a house
settings.by: The LORD, speaking to Moses and Aaron
settings.to: Spoken to Moses and Aaron (14:33), about the Israelites who will own houses in Canaan. The owner reports and the priest inspects (14:35).
settings.when: For the future: when you come into the land of Canaan (14:34)
settings.why: This law cannot apply in the camp of tents; it looks ahead to houses of stone in the land. It tells the owner and the priest how to deal with spreading mold. The steps run from scraping and new plaster to tearing the house down. Its setting is a reminder that the book speaks to a people on the way.

title: The Body's Flows
sum: Chapter 15 deals with discharges from the sexual organs, in four parts arranged like a mirror: a man's abnormal discharge, a man's emission of seed, a woman's monthly period, and a woman's abnormal bleeding. Each makes a person unclean, and the uncleanness spreads to beds, seats, saddles and those who touch them. The normal cases last until evening or seven days and need only washing; the abnormal ones need seven clean days and two birds on the eighth. The reason is stated at the end: so that Israel will not "die in their uncleanness by making my tabernacle that is among them unclean."
Nothing here calls the body or sex sinful, but God's dwelling among the people means the most private parts of life are kept apart from the holy.

views.H: Laws of bodily purity for the camp around the tabernacle, applied later to the temple and Jerusalem.
views.C: A carefully built Priestly composition; the Holiness writers later turned the menstrual rule into a moral ban (18:19; 20:18).
views.A: Milgrom's life-and-death reading: semen and blood are life leaving the body. Douglas: the body's openings are boundaries, like the camp's, that must be guarded.
views.J: The basis of the laws of niddah and the mikveh, kept in Orthodox Judaism as "family purity" (taharat ha-mishpachah).
views.X: Jesus heals a woman bleeding for twelve years who touched him (Mark 5:25–34). Gregory the Great allowed menstruating women to enter church and receive communion.

deep.b: Most of the laws of chapters 11–15 required a sanctuary, so when the Temple fell they lapsed. Two survived strongly in Judaism: the food laws of chapter 11, and the laws of niddah, which the rabbis tied to the ban in 18:19 and extended. Observant couples still keep apart during the period and for seven clean days after it, and the wife immerses in a mikveh. Women's experiences of the practice vary widely, and Jewish feminist writers have both defended and criticized it. In Christianity, the purity laws were generally read as fulfilled or set aside, though some churches long kept customs of purification after childbirth ("churching").

echoes: Exodus 19:15; Numbers 5:1–4; Numbers 19:11–22; Deuteronomy 23:10–11; 1 Samuel 21:4–5; Ezekiel 36:17; Mark 5:25–34; Mark 7:1–5

settings.what: The laws of bodily discharges
settings.by: The LORD, speaking to Moses and Aaron
settings.to: The Israelites (15:2): every man and woman, and husbands and wives together
settings.when: At Sinai, for life in the camp
settings.why: To deal with the normal and abnormal flows of the body, which make a person unclean for a time. Washing and waiting end the uncleanness, and long illnesses also need offerings. The purpose is stated in 15:31: so that the Israelites do not die by making the tabernacle among them unclean. Uncleanness is not sin, but it must be kept away from God's dwelling.
views: Jewish law built the laws of family purity on 15:19–24 and 18:19; Christian readers have mostly treated them as ceremonial.

title: The Day of Atonement
sum: After the death of Aaron's sons God sets the terms for entering the inner room: not at any time, but once a year, in plain linen, with a cloud of incense to hide the atonement lid, and with blood. Aaron offers a bull for himself and his household. Two goats are chosen by lot, one "for the LORD" and one "for Azazel." The blood of the bull and of the LORD's goat is spattered on and before the lid, then on the altar, to cleanse the sanctuary of Israel's uncleanness and rebellions. Then Aaron leans both hands on the live goat, confesses all Israel's sins over it, and sends it into the wilderness. On the tenth of the seventh month the people must humble themselves and rest, "for on this day he will make atonement for you, to make you clean."

Chapter 16 is the center of Leviticus and, for many, of the whole Torah. It gathers up the sin offering, the purity laws and the high priesthood into one day when God's house and God's people are made clean.
readings: Read as cleansing the sanctuary
Following Milgrom, the blood purges God's house of the year's pollution, so that he can stay among his people, and the live goat carries away the people's sins.
Read as the gospel in shadow
Hebrews 9–10: Christ, high priest and offering, enters the true holy place once for all with his own blood, and the goat carrying sin away pictures his taking away the world's sin (John 1:29).
Read as the day of return
In Judaism the day has become one of fasting, confession and repentance, ending in assurance: "Who makes you clean? Your Father in heaven" (Mishnah Yoma 8:9).

views.H: The annual rite of the wilderness tabernacle and of the temple, described in detail in the Mishnah tractate Yoma.
views.C: Many critics see layers: an old elimination rite (the goat for Azazel), a Priestly purging of the sanctuary, and the later annual date and fast (16:29–34). Ezekiel 45:18–20 has a different calendar of cleansing.
views.A: Two movements, inward (blood carried into the center) and outward (sin carried into the wilderness), restore the map of holy and common, clean and unclean.
views.J: Yom Kippur: the Avodah service retells the high priest's day, the Torah reading is Leviticus 16, the afternoon reading is chapter 18, and the book of Jonah teaches repentance.
views.X: Hebrews 9:1–10:18 is a sustained reading of this chapter; Romans 3:25 calls Christ the hilastērion; Good Friday is often linked to it.

deep.b:
In the Second Temple the day became a great public drama. The Mishnah tells how the high priest was kept awake the night before, swore to follow the Pharisees' ruling on the incense, bathed five times, entered the inner room four times, and pronounced the divine name in confession while the people fell on their faces (Yoma 1–7). Sirach 50 describes the high priest Simon, perhaps on this day, coming out "like the morning star among the clouds." At Qumran the community kept the day by its own calendar, and a commentary on Habakkuk says the "Wicked Priest" attacked their teacher on it (1QpHab 11:4–8).

After AD 70 Judaism replaced the rite with prayer: the five services of Yom Kippur, the confessions, the Avodah poems that relive the temple service, and the closing Ne'ilah. Christianity read the chapter through Hebrews: Christ the high priest, the cross the altar, heaven the true holy place, and the torn veil (Mark 15:38) the way opened to all.

echoes: Exodus 25:17–22; Exodus 30:10; Exodus 33:20; Isaiah 53:4–12; Ezekiel 45:18–20; Zechariah 3:1–5; Sirach 50:5–21; John 1:29; Romans 3:25; Hebrews 9:1–28; Hebrews 10:1–22; Hebrews 13:11–13

settings.what: The rite of the Day of Atonement
settings.to: Aaron, the high priest, through Moses (16:2): "Tell your brother Aaron"
settings.when: After the death of Aaron's two sons (16:1); at Sinai
settings.why: To tell the high priest how he may enter the inner room behind the veil without dying. He comes once a year, in linen, with blood and incense. He cleanses the sanctuary, the tent and the altar. Then he sends the goat for Azazel into the wilderness carrying Israel's sins. This answers the problem that runs through chapters 1–15. Impurity and sin build up where God lives, and they must be cleared away.
views: Milgrom: 16:1–28 may first have been a rite for times of crisis, made yearly by 16:29–34.
A wilderness demon, a place name, or 'the goat that goes away': see the note on 16:8.

settings.what: The yearly day: humble yourselves
settings.to: All the Israelites, the native-born and the foreigner living among them (16:29)
settings.when: Every year on the tenth day of the seventh month, for all time
settings.why: To turn the high priest's rite into a day for the whole people. They do no work, and they humble themselves (fasting, in Jewish practice). The priest makes atonement; the people take part by rest and self-denial. This is the source of Yom Kippur.
views: Knohl and Milgrom: these verses come from the Holiness school, which drew the people into a rite that had belonged to the priest.

traditions.q: How does Christ's death fulfill the Day of Atonement?
views: Christ took the punishment that sinners deserved, as the goat bore the people's sins away, and so fully satisfied God's justice (Calvin, Institutes 2.16; Westminster Confession 8.5). This is the view called penal substitution.

Christ bore the curse of the law in our place (Galatians 3:13) and his obedience is counted to believers (Formula of Concord, article 3). The Swedish Lutheran bishop Gustaf Aulén argued that the oldest Christian view is Christ's victory over sin, death and the devil, and many Lutherans now hold both.

Christ's death is the one perfect sacrifice, offered out of love, which makes satisfaction for the sins of all (Catechism 613–617). Catholic theology, following Aquinas, stresses Christ's loving obedience offered to the Father more than God punishing the Son.

Christ entered death to destroy it and to heal human nature from within. Orthodox writers usually avoid saying that God needed to punish sin before he could forgive, and stress the resurrection as part of the atonement.

Leviticus 16 maps Christ's work in heaven. He made atonement on the cross, and since 1844 he has carried out a final phase of judgment and cleansing in the heavenly sanctuary (Daniel 8:14; Hebrews 8–9; Fundamental Beliefs 24). Adventists identify the goat for Azazel with Satan, who bears his own guilt at the end.
